question: Action Comics issue #1, published in 1938, featured the debut of the most famous superhero in history. Who?
context: Created by Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster, both teenagers from Cleveland. The first issue cost ten cents; a pristine copy sold for $6 million in 2024.

question: Detective Comics #27 in 1939 introduced a millionaire who fights crime in a bat costume. What's his secret identity?
context: Bob Kane is credited as creator but writer Bill Finger contributed the cape, cowl, and detective elements; DC formally added Finger's credit in 2015.

question: Captain America #1 in March 1941 featured a now-iconic cover. Who was Cap punching on it?
context: Joe Simon and Jack Kirby created Cap nine months before Pearl Harbor. The cover drew angry letters from American Nazi sympathizers; NYC mayor Fiorello La Guardia personally called the publisher to offer police protection.

question: Amazing Fantasy #15 in August 1962 introduced a teenager bitten by a radioactive spider. What's his name?
context: Written by Stan Lee, drawn by Steve Ditko. Publisher Martin Goodman thought spiders were creepy and gave Spider-Man only one issue to fail. Sales were so good Spidey got his own title four months later.

question: Fantastic Four #1 in 1961 kicked off the Marvel Silver Age. Who were the two creators?
context: Lee wrote, Kirby drew. The team — Mr. Fantastic, Invisible Girl, Human Torch, Thing — got their powers from cosmic-ray exposure on a rocket flight.

question: What metal is Wolverine's skeleton and claws made of?
context: Wolverine debuted in Incredible Hulk #181 in 1974. The adamantium-bonding was done forcibly to Logan by the Weapon X program. Vibranium is Captain America's shield metal.

question: Wonder Woman first appeared in 1941. Her creator was a Harvard-trained psychologist who also invented an important real-world device. What did he invent?
context: William Moulton Marston also lived with two women in a polyamorous relationship that informed his ideas about female-led utopian societies. Wonder Woman's Lasso of Truth is a direct nod to the polygraph.

question: Stan Lee co-created dozens of Marvel heroes in the 1960s. What was his signature sign-off catchphrase?
context: Lee used 'Excelsior' from the Latin for 'ever upward' — also the New York State motto. He'd often close his Stan's Soapbox columns with it. Lee died in 2018 at 95.

question: Jack Kirby drew X-Men, Avengers, and Fantastic Four for Marvel in the 1960s. What was his industry nickname?
context: Kirby is widely considered the most influential American comics artist of all time. He also co-created Captain America in 1941 with Joe Simon. His dynamic 'Kirby Krackle' visual style for cosmic energy is still imitated.

question: The X-Men's bald telepathic leader founded a school for mutants in Westchester, NY. What's his name?
context: Xavier and Magneto's friendship-turned-rivalry was loosely modeled by Stan Lee on Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. The school is at the Xavier Institute in Salem Center, New York.

question: Spider-Man's most famous principle, taught to Peter by his Uncle Ben, is what?
answer: With great power comes great responsibility
choices: With great power comes great responsibility
Never let your guard down against true evil
The strong have a duty to protect the weak
A hero's job is to never stop trying his best
context: The line appears in the closing caption of Amazing Fantasy #15. Uncle Ben's death — Peter failing to stop a burglar who later kills Ben — is the moment that launches Spider-Man's career.

question: Thor's enchanted hammer in Marvel Comics is called what?
context: Thor first appeared in Journey into Mystery #83 in 1962. Only the worthy can lift Mjolnir. Stormbreaker is a separate hammer wielded by Beta Ray Bill.

question: Harry Potter's wizarding school is called what?
answer: Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry
choices: Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry
context: Hogwarts is in the Scottish Highlands. Beauxbatons is French and Durmstrang is Northern European — both featured in Goblet of Fire. Author JK Rowling wrote the first book in Edinburgh cafés.

question: Harry Potter's main villain is a Dark Lord whose name most wizards refuse to say. What is his name?
context: His birth name was Tom Marvolo Riddle, an anagram of 'I am Lord Voldemort.' Most characters call him 'You-Know-Who' or 'He Who Must Not Be Named.' Harry's distinctive lightning-bolt scar comes from Voldemort's failed killing curse in 1981.

question: Harry Potter is sorted into what Hogwarts house?
context: The Sorting Hat almost places Harry in Slytherin but listens to his preference. Gryffindor was founded by Godric Gryffindor; its colors are scarlet and gold, its animal a lion.

question: The Harry Potter books, written in Edinburgh cafés in the 1990s, are by which British author?
context: Joanne Rowling famously wrote much of the first book as a single mother on welfare. The publisher added the 'K' (for her grandmother Kathleen, a name she never had) so the books would appeal to boys.

question: What's the name of Harry Potter's pet snowy owl?
context: Hagrid buys Hedwig for Harry as an 11th birthday gift in Diagon Alley. Errol is the Weasleys' owl, Pigwidgeon is Ron's, Crookshanks is Hermione's cat.

question: The headmaster of Hogwarts for most of the Harry Potter series is what wizard with a long silver beard?
context: Dumbledore's full name is Albus Percival Wulfric Brian Dumbledore. He defeated the dark wizard Grindelwald in 1945 and is considered the greatest wizard of his age.

question: Harry Potter's two best friends at Hogwarts are Ron Weasley and what bookish girl?
context: Hermione is a Muggle-born witch and the top student in their year. The trio meets on the Hogwarts Express in 1991. Hermione's name is pronounced 'her-MY-oh-nee.'

question: Quidditch is the wizarding sport in Harry Potter. What position does Harry play for Gryffindor?
context: The Seeker chases the Golden Snitch — a tiny winged ball worth 150 points. Catching it usually ends the match. Harry becomes the youngest Seeker in a century when he joins the team as a first year.

question: Harry Potter's Hogwarts-friendly half-giant gamekeeper, who first delivers Harry to Hogwarts, is named what?
context: Hagrid was expelled from Hogwarts as a student in 1943 but allowed to stay as gamekeeper through Dumbledore's intervention. He raises everything from acromantulas to dragons.

question: Harry Potter's Patronus, the animal form of his protective spell, is what?
context: The Patronus Charm is taught in Prisoner of Azkaban. Harry's stag is the form his father James also took as an Animagus. Hermione's Patronus is an otter (Rowling's favorite animal); Ron's is a Jack Russell terrier.

question: Robert Downey Jr. played which Marvel hero in the 2008 film that launched the MCU?
context: Jon Favreau directed the 2008 Iron Man. The casting of Downey — then still recovering from drug-related arrests — was a massive gamble that set the MCU's wisecracking tone for over a decade.

question: Which actor played Captain America in the MCU from 2011 through Endgame?
context: Evans had previously played the Human Torch in the 2005 Fantastic Four films. He almost turned down Captain America: The First Avenger before agreeing to a multi-film contract.

question: In Avengers: Infinity War (2018), the villain who collects Infinity Stones is named what?
context: Thanos is played by Josh Brolin via motion capture. His name comes from Thanatos, Greek god of death. He first appeared in Marvel Comics in 1973 created by Jim Starlin.

question: Chris Hemsworth plays which Asgardian hero across nine MCU appearances?
context: Hemsworth was nearly cut from auditions; his brother Liam read for the part before Chris's mother pushed him to try again. Kenneth Branagh directed the 2011 Thor.

question: Tom Hiddleston plays which trickster god across many MCU films?
context: Hiddleston originally auditioned for Thor before being cast as Loki. Loki is Thor's adopted brother — actually a Frost Giant raised in Asgard by Odin. He invades New York with the Chitauri in 2012's The Avengers.

question: The team of misfit space heroes in the 2014 MCU film led by Star-Lord is called what?
choices: The Inhumans Royal Family of Attilan
context: Directed by James Gunn. The team includes Star-Lord (Chris Pratt), Gamora, Drax, Rocket Raccoon, and Groot ('I am Groot'). The soundtrack of 1970s pop hits became iconic.

question: What 2018 MCU film, directed by Ryan Coogler, was set in the African nation of Wakanda?
context: Chadwick Boseman starred as T'Challa. The film grossed over $1.3 billion and received seven Oscar nominations including Best Picture — a first for a superhero film. Boseman died of cancer in 2020.

question: Mark Ruffalo took over the role of the Hulk in 2012 from Edward Norton (who played him in 2008). What's the Hulk's civilian name?
context: Eric Bana played Banner in 2003's Hulk before Norton's 2008 version and then Ruffalo's. Banner's transformation is triggered by anger; he becomes the green-skinned Hulk after a gamma-radiation accident.

question: In 1956, DC Comics rebooted The Flash in Showcase #4 with a new secret identity replacing Jay Garrick's. This issue is widely credited with launching the Silver Age of comics. What was the new Flash's name?
answer: Barry Allen, the police forensic scientist
choices: Barry Allen, the police forensic scientist
Wally West, Barry's nephew and protégé
Bart Allen, the speedster from the future
Jay Garrick, the original 1940s Flash returning
context: Barry's costume — red with yellow lightning — was designed by Carmine Infantino. He was struck by lightning and doused in chemicals in his crime lab. Wally West would take over the mantle decades later after Crisis on Infinite Earths in 1985.

question: Hal Jordan became the Silver Age Green Lantern in 1959 after a dying alien gave him a powerful green ring. What's the organization Hal joined?
context: The Corps is a force of 7,200 intergalactic peacekeepers run by the Guardians of the Universe on the planet Oa. Hal Jordan was a test pilot when the dying Abin Sur passed him the ring. The Corps oath: 'In brightest day, in blackest night...'

question: Jack Kirby and Stan Lee created the X-Men in 1963 with five original members. Who was the team's red-eyebeam-firing field leader?
context: Scott Summers can't control his optic blasts, so he wears a ruby-quartz visor or glasses. The five original X-Men were Cyclops, Marvel Girl (Jean Grey), Angel, Beast, and Iceman. The team was repeatedly cancelled and revived until Giant-Size X-Men #1 in 1975.

question: Daredevil first appeared in 1964 in his own title from Marvel. He's blinded as a young man by radioactive waste that paradoxically boosts his other senses to superhuman levels. What's his civilian profession?
answer: Lawyer in Hell's Kitchen, New York
choices: Lawyer in Hell's Kitchen, New York
context: Matt Murdock practices law with partner Foggy Nelson at Nelson & Murdock. Created by Stan Lee and Bill Everett, Daredevil first appeared in Daredevil #1, April 1964. Frank Miller's late-1970s/early-1980s run redefined the character.

question: In Fantastic Four #52 (1966), Stan Lee and Jack Kirby introduced the first mainstream black superhero — the king of an African nation called Wakanda. Who?
choices: Storm of the Mau Mau kingdom
Luke Cage of Harlem's hero scene
context: The Black Panther Party in California formed independently around the same time. Marvel briefly renamed the character 'Black Leopard' in 1972 to avoid confusion before reverting. T'Challa rules a technologically advanced, vibranium-rich nation.

question: Wolverine first appeared in 1974, debuted his full backstory in Giant-Size X-Men #1 in 1975, and is famous for being short and angry. Created by Len Wein and John Romita Sr., what's the character's real name?
context: Wolverine first appeared in Incredible Hulk #181, October 1974, fighting both Hulk and Wendigo. His real name was revealed gradually — 'Logan' became canon in Uncanny X-Men, the full 'James Howlett' came in the 2001 Origin miniseries.

question: Chris Claremont wrote X-Men from 1975 to 1991, a record-setting 16-year run that defined the modern team. What was his most famous arc, drawn by John Byrne, in which Jean Grey is consumed by cosmic power?
context: Dark Phoenix ran in Uncanny X-Men #129–137. Editor Jim Shooter required Claremont and Byrne to change the original ending — Phoenix's destruction of an inhabited solar system mandated her death. Byrne later left the book.

question: Alan Moore's 12-issue Watchmen (1986–87) features an iconic recurring image that appears on the cover of issue #1 and many times throughout the series. What is it?
answer: A yellow smiley-face button with a blood splatter across one eye
choices: A yellow smiley-face button with a blood splatter across one eye
A red rose held by a costumed vigilante in silhouette
A black silhouette of a clock with hands at midnight
A blue silhouette of a man against a glowing red moon
context: The smiley face belongs to the murdered Comedian (Edward Blake), whose death opens the series. Dave Gibbons drew the entire 12 issues. The smiley face is also used in Watchmen's nine-panel grid system, the Doomsday Clock, and Mars sequences.

question: Frank Miller's 1986 four-issue prestige series for DC depicted a 55-year-old Bruce Wayne coming out of retirement in a dystopian Gotham. What was the series called?
context: Miller followed up in 1987 with Year One (Batman's first year, with David Mazzucchelli). The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen, both from 1986, are often cited as the start of the 'mature' comics era. Miller's older Batman fights a returning Joker, a Reagan-allied Superman, and the Mutant gang leader.

question: Neil Gaiman's Sandman ran for 75 issues from 1989 to 1996 and centered on Dream, also known as Morpheus, lord of all stories. Dream is one of seven siblings called the Endless. Who is the eldest, the smiling but rarely seen sister?
context: The seven Endless: Destiny, Death, Dream, Destruction, Desire, Despair, and Delirium (formerly Delight). Death appears as a cheerful young goth woman with an Egyptian ankh necklace. The series won 26 Eisner Awards and the World Fantasy Award for short fiction in 1991.

question: Mike Mignola created a red-skinned, horn-stubbed, cigar-smoking demon-detective for Dark Horse Comics in 1993. What's the character called?
context: Hellboy was summoned to Earth by Nazi occultists in 1944 but raised by Allied paranormal researcher Trevor Bruttenholm. He works for the Bureau for Paranormal Research and Defense (BPRD). Guillermo del Toro directed the 2004 and 2008 films starring Ron Perlman.

question: Garth Ennis and Steve Dillon ran Preacher from 1995 to 2000 at DC's Vertigo imprint. The hero is a small-town Texas pastor who gains a divine voice that can command obedience. His traveling companions are his on-and-off girlfriend Tulip and what Irish vampire?
context: Jesse Custer, the preacher, hosts an entity called Genesis — offspring of an angel and a demon. The trio crosses America hunting God Himself, who has abandoned creation. AMC adapted the comic into a four-season TV series in 2016–2019.

question: The first Harry Potter book was published in the UK in 1997 under one title and in the US under a different title. What was the British original called?
answer: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
choices: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
Harry Potter and the Magic Stone
Harry Potter and the First Year
context: US publisher Scholastic insisted on changing 'Philosopher's' to 'Sorcerer's' for the 1998 American release, worried 'philosopher' sounded too academic. The Philosopher's Stone is a real alchemical concept tied to Nicolas Flamel, a real 14th-century French alchemist who features in the book.

question: Harry Potter's mentor figure throughout the early years at Hogwarts is the Potions Master who later turns out to be a complex double agent. Who is he?
context: Snape is head of Slytherin House. He famously taunts Harry from the first day of Potions class. Alan Rickman played him in all eight films; Rickman knew Snape's full arc from Rowling earlier than the cast or readers did.

question: In Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, Harry meets his godfather — a wrongly accused convict who escaped from the wizard prison Azkaban. Who is he?
context: Sirius can transform into a large black dog, his Animagus form. He was framed for betraying Harry's parents by Peter Pettigrew (Wormtail). Sirius dies in Order of the Phoenix (book five), killed by Bellatrix Lestrange and falling through the Veil in the Department of Mysteries.

question: The Marauder's Map in Harry Potter shows the location of every person in Hogwarts. What phrase activates it, and what closes it?
answer: 'I solemnly swear that I am up to no good' / 'Mischief managed'
choices: 'I solemnly swear that I am up to no good' / 'Mischief managed'
'Show me what is hidden' / 'Concealed once more'
context: The Map was made by the Marauders: Moony (Remus Lupin), Wormtail (Peter Pettigrew), Padfoot (Sirius Black), and Prongs (James Potter). Fred and George Weasley give it to Harry in Prisoner of Azkaban after stealing it from Filch's office.

question: What rare flying creature does Hagrid bring to Harry's Care of Magical Creatures class in Prisoner of Azkaban, which Harry must approach with a deep bow?
context: A Hippogriff has the front half of an eagle and the back half of a horse. Buckbeak is sentenced to death after attacking Draco Malfoy (who didn't bow). Harry and Hermione later use Hermione's Time-Turner to rescue Buckbeak.

question: Goblet of Fire (book 4) features the Triwizard Tournament between Hogwarts, Beauxbatons, and Durmstrang. What ends the third task, when Harry and Cedric Diggory grab the Triwizard Cup at the same moment?
answer: They are Portkey-transported to a graveyard where Voldemort returns
choices: They are Portkey-transported to a graveyard where Voldemort returns
They are dropped into a flooded chamber to face a sea giant
They are sent back to Hogwarts where the Cup explodes
They are transported to the Forbidden Forest for a centaur trial
context: Cedric Diggory is killed by Peter Pettigrew on Voldemort's orders. Voldemort uses Harry's blood for his resurrection. Mad-Eye Moody (actually Barty Crouch Jr. on Polyjuice) had turned the Cup into a Portkey. Robert Pattinson played Cedric in the 2005 film.

question: The five Hogwarts houses are Gryffindor, Slytherin, Ravenclaw, Hufflepuff. Wait — Hogwarts has only four. Who was the founder of Slytherin House?
context: Slytherin valued cunning and pure-blood ancestry, leading to his split with the other founders. He sealed a basilisk in the Chamber of Secrets — discovered by Tom Riddle in 1942 and reopened in 1992. Slytherin's symbol is a serpent; house colors are green and silver.

question: In Chamber of Secrets, the petrified students of Hogwarts are saved when Harry kills the basilisk and pierces what enchanted object Tom Riddle had been using to possess Ginny Weasley?
context: The diary is the first Horcrux destroyed — Harry stabs it with the basilisk fang. The seven Horcruxes total: diary, ring, locket, cup, diadem, Nagini, and an unintended one Harry only learns about in book seven.

question: Alfonso Cuarón directed which Harry Potter film, bringing a notably darker visual style and influencing every film after it?
answer: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004)
choices: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004)
Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone (2001)
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2005)
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (2007)
context: Chris Columbus directed the first two; Cuarón did Azkaban; Mike Newell did Goblet of Fire; David Yates directed the last four films. Cuarón's work on Azkaban led to his later acclaim for Children of Men (2006), Gravity (2013), and Roma (2018).

question: Dumbledore's pet phoenix at Hogwarts, named after a Christian medieval saint, is what color?
answer: Crimson and gold (with a long golden tail)
choices: Crimson and gold (with a long golden tail)
Silver and white with platinum-tipped wings
Black and purple with iridescent feathers
context: Fawkes is named for the English Catholic conspirator Guy Fawkes (Gunpowder Plot, November 5, 1605). The phoenix's tears heal Harry's basilisk wound in Chamber of Secrets. Phoenix tail feathers are wand cores — Harry's and Voldemort's wands both contain feathers from Fawkes.

question: Iron Man (2008), directed by Jon Favreau, established the MCU template. In the post-credits scene, Nick Fury appears to Tony Stark and mentions launching what initiative?
context: Samuel L. Jackson played Fury based on his depiction in Mark Millar's Ultimate Marvel comics, which had drawn Fury as Jackson. The scene was added late and cost Jackson a one-day shoot to film. The Avengers (2012) arrived four years later.

question: Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014) introduced the directing brothers who would later helm Civil War, Infinity War, and Endgame. What are their names?
context: The Russos came from TV comedy (Arrested Development, Community). The Winter Soldier was their first major film. They earned the Infinity War / Endgame gig partly on the 70s-political-thriller tone they brought to Cap 2.

question: Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy (2014) features a 1970s-pop-rock soundtrack on a cassette tape Star-Lord carries from Earth. What's the in-universe name of the mix?
context: The mix tape was made by Peter Quill's mother before her death. Songs include 'Hooked on a Feeling' (Blue Swede), 'Come and Get Your Love' (Redbone), and 'I Want You Back' (Jackson 5). James Gunn personally selected every track from his own 70s collection.

question: Thor: Ragnarok (2017) was directed by which New Zealand filmmaker, who also voiced the soft-spoken rock-monster gladiator Korg?
context: Waititi had directed Hunt for the Wilderpeople (2016) and What We Do in the Shadows (2014). Ragnarok rebooted Thor's tone toward broad comedy, introduced Tessa Thompson as Valkyrie and Cate Blanchett as Hela, and ended Asgard's existence as a place.

question: Avengers: Infinity War (2018) climaxes with Thanos snapping his fingers using all six Infinity Stones, vaporizing half of all life. Spider-Man's final words to Tony Stark as he disintegrates have become an iconic line. What does Peter say?
answer: I don't feel so good, Mr. Stark
choices: I don't feel so good, Mr. Stark
Tell Aunt May I'm sorry, Mr. Stark
What's happening to me, Mr. Stark?
I don't want to go, Mr. Stark, I don't want to go
context: Tom Holland reportedly improvised much of the scene; the Russos asked him to play Peter as a scared kid. The line plays on Peter's youth — he isn't ready for what's happening. Holland delivered the line on-set with Robert Downey Jr. only, no green screen.

question: In Avengers: Endgame (2019), Captain America delivers a line during the final battle that recalls a 1960s Avengers comics catchphrase. What does Steve Rogers say?
context: It's the first time Cap says the full phrase in any MCU film, after the Russos held it back for 22 movies. Stan Lee coined 'Avengers Assemble!' in the comics in the 1960s. The line cues the portal-scene return of every dusted hero.

question: In Endgame, who wields Mjolnir during the final battle against Thanos, having proven worthy in Avengers: Age of Ultron when he made it twitch?
context: In Age of Ultron, Cap makes Mjolnir budge at a party, hinting he was secretly worthy. The Russos waited four years to pay off the joke. Chris Evans's reaction shot when he wields it — Thor's stunned 'I knew it!' — is one of Endgame's biggest crowd moments.

question: Robert Downey Jr.'s Tony Stark delivers a final four-word line in Endgame, echoing the arc-opening reveal from Iron Man (2008). What does he say before snapping with the Infinity Stones?
context: Tony's 2008 'I am Iron Man' press-conference reveal made Iron Man's identity public — totally inverting comics' usual secret-identity setup. Tony's Endgame line is a bookend; the snap kills Thanos and his army but proves fatal to Tony. Pepper Potts (Gwyneth Paltrow) is at his side as he dies.

question: Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster sold Superman to DC Comics in 1938 for $130 — splitting $65 each — alongside a 10-year contract. The character generated tens of millions for DC over the following decades while Siegel and Shuster lived in poverty. The duo sued DC in the late 1940s and lost. What 1975 development finally got DC to begin paying them small annual stipends?
answer: The publicity campaign around the 1978 Richard Donner Superman film
choices: The publicity campaign around the 1978 Richard Donner Superman film
A successful 1975 federal lawsuit against Warner Bros. parent company
The 1976 Marvel-DC settlement on shared character rights
The 1975 founding of the Comics Industry Code authority for credit
context: Neal Adams led a public-pressure campaign that embarrassed DC ahead of Superman: The Movie. DC settled with each surviving creator for $20,000 a year and 'creators of Superman' credit on all subsequent uses. Both Siegel (died 1996) and Shuster (died 1992) finally got their names on Superman's stories.

question: In 1992, DC Comics killed Superman in a now-legendary storyline. The death is dealt by a hulking gray monster that emerged from a meteor crater and fought through the Justice League. Issue #75 of Superman included a poster-bag and a black armband. What was the monster's name?
context: Dan Jurgens created Doomsday and wrote and drew the death issue. The body count grand finale (Superman #75, January 1993) sold over 3 million copies. Superman returned a few months later via four 'replacements' — Steel, Superboy, Cyborg Superman, and the Eradicator — before the real Superman emerged from a Kryptonian regeneration matrix.

question: Frank Miller's celebrated Daredevil run (1979–1983, then 1986's Born Again with David Mazzucchelli) introduced a deadly assassin who was Matt Murdock's college girlfriend, hired by the Kingpin, and dies impaled on her own sai by Bullseye. What's her name?
context: Elektra first appeared in Daredevil #168 (January 1981). Miller killed her in #181 over Marvel editorial protest. He was assured she'd stay dead. She came back a few years later. Jennifer Garner played her in Daredevil (2003) and Elektra (2005); Élodie Yung played her in the Netflix Daredevil series.

question: Alan Moore wrote The Killing Joke for DC in 1988, drawn by Brian Bolland — a 48-page Batman one-shot exploring the Joker's possible origin as a failed comedian forced into a chemical bath. The book is notorious for the brutal attack on which character?
answer: Barbara Gordon, Batgirl and Commissioner Gordon's daughter
choices: Barbara Gordon, Batgirl and Commissioner Gordon's daughter
Vicki Vale, the Gotham Globe photojournalist
Selina Kyle, Catwoman in her Earth-2 incarnation
Talia al Ghul, daughter of Ra's al Ghul
context: The Joker shoots Barbara through the spine, paralyzing her. Moore later expressed regret over how the book treated her. Barbara reinvented herself as the computer hacker Oracle, written prominently in Birds of Prey. The 'one bad day' premise — anyone could become the Joker — is the philosophical core of the book.

question: Crisis on Infinite Earths (1985–86) was DC's 12-issue maxi-series that erased decades of parallel-Earth continuity. Written by Marv Wolfman and drawn by George Pérez, it featured the death of two major heroes: Supergirl and what speedster who sacrificed himself running the Anti-Monitor to death?
context: Barry's death in Crisis #8 was meant to be permanent. Wally West, his nephew and former Kid Flash, took over as the Flash for 20 years until Geoff Johns brought Barry back in Final Crisis (2008–09). Pérez drew the Crisis covers; he passed away in May 2022.

question: Jim Starlin and George Pérez's Infinity Gauntlet (1991) was a six-issue maxi-series where the Mad Titan Thanos assembles six gems on a gauntlet and wipes out half of all life with a snap. Marvel adapted the broad concept for Avengers: Infinity War. What does Thanos do, in the comic, that triggers the heroes' counterattack?
answer: He erases his beloved Death by accident while showing off, then must restore her
choices: He erases his beloved Death by accident while showing off, then must restore her
He challenges Galactus to a duel and consumes a small planet inhabited by orks
He releases Adam Warlock from the Soul Gem prematurely, who turns on him
He calls down Mephisto to bring Earth's remaining heroes into the underworld
context: Thanos's lifelong courtship of Death (personified as a hooded woman in the comics) doesn't make it into the movies. The gauntlet has six gems: Soul, Time, Space, Mind, Reality, Power. Pérez drew the first three issues; Ron Lim completed the series after Pérez's deadline crunch.

question: In Mark Millar and Steve McNiven's Civil War (2006–07), the U.S. government passes the Superhuman Registration Act, splitting heroes between pro-registration and anti-registration factions. Iron Man leads the pro side; Captain America leads the anti side. The series ends with Cap's surrender — and his subsequent assassination by what character on the courthouse steps?
answer: Crossbones (Brock Rumlow), then Sharon Carter under mind control
choices: Crossbones (Brock Rumlow), then Sharon Carter under mind control
Bullseye (Lester) hired by Norman Osborn for the Thunderbolts
The Punisher (Frank Castle) caught between sides
The Red Skull personally with a Cosmic Cube
context: Crossbones fires the initial sniper round; Sharon Carter (Cap's girlfriend, brainwashed by Doctor Faustus) delivers the killing shot. Cap's body is shown on the steps of the Federal Courthouse in Manhattan. Bucky Barnes (Winter Soldier) takes up the shield. The 2007 Captain America #25 sold out within hours.

question: Ed Brubaker's Captain America run (2004–2012) brought back Bucky Barnes, Cap's WWII sidekick. Bucky had been presumed dead since 1945, but Brubaker revealed the Soviets had recovered his body, given him a metal arm, and used him as a cryogenically frozen assassin for decades. What was his Soviet code name?
context: Brubaker's Winter Soldier arc, with Steve Epting on art, ran in Captain America (vol. 5) #1–14 (2005). The Russos adapted it as Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014), starring Sebastian Stan as Bucky. The metal arm in the comic was originally bionic-Cyborg; the films changed it to vibranium with kinetic-pulse functions.

question: Jeff Smith self-published Bone from 1991 to 2004 through his own Cartoon Books — a 1,300-page black-and-white epic following three cartoon-looking cousins lost in a sword-and-sorcery world. The three cousins are Fone Bone, Smiley Bone, and what greedy schemer?
answer: Phoney Bone (real name Phoncible P. Bone)
choices: Phoney Bone (real name Phoncible P. Bone)
Sneaky Bone (real name Sneakford P. Bone)
Cranky Bone (real name Crankford T. Bone)
Bouncy Bone (real name Boungo T. Bone)
context: Smith was inspired by Walt Kelly's Pogo, Carl Barks's Donald Duck, and Tolkien's Lord of the Rings in roughly equal parts. The series won a record-setting 11 Eisner Awards and 10 Harvey Awards. Scholastic later released the books in color.

question: Frank Miller's 1991 Sin City was published in black-and-white at Dark Horse Comics, a noir crime saga set in Basin City. The first story 'The Hard Goodbye' centered on a hulking, deformed ex-con named what, who hunts the killer of his one-night stand Goldie?
context: Mickey Rourke played Marv in Robert Rodriguez and Frank Miller's 2005 Sin City film, with Bruce Willis as Hartigan and Clive Owen as Dwight. Miller's hand-drawn high-contrast art with selective color washes (yellow Roark Jr., red Goldie blood) became the film's visual signature.

question: Frank Miller's 1998 historical-comic 300, published by Dark Horse, dramatized the Battle of Thermopylae (480 BC) where 300 Spartans under King Leonidas held the pass against Xerxes's Persian army. Zack Snyder directed the 2007 film. The Spartan king's most quoted line, as he kicks a Persian envoy into a pit, is what?
context: The actual ancient quote, from Plutarch and Herodotus, was 'Molon labe' — 'Come and take them' — Leonidas's reply when Xerxes demanded the Spartans surrender their weapons. Gerard Butler played Leonidas in the film. The 'spartan kick' meme of dropkicking someone into darkness became one of the most reused 2000s internet jokes.

question: Mark Waid and Alex Ross's 1996 Kingdom Come, a four-issue Elseworlds prestige series for DC, depicts an aged Superman returning to leadership after years of retirement. The narrative is framed through the eyes of a small-town pastor experiencing apocalyptic dreams, who turns out to be guided by what biblical-named DC hero?
choices: Doctor Fate (with the Helmet of Nabu)
context: Alex Ross painted every page; Mark Waid wrote. The visual style — fully painted realistic figures — was inspired by Norman Rockwell. Pastor Norman McCay is modeled on Ross's father, a real-life Methodist minister. The series ended with Superman returning to a normal life and Wonder Woman pregnant.

question: In Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (book 5, 2003), Harry, Ron, Hermione, and friends form a secret defense-against-the-dark-arts study group in defiance of Hogwarts' Ministry-appointed instructor Dolores Umbridge. What do they call themselves?
context: The group meets in the Room of Requirement, a magically-revealed chamber on the seventh floor. Hermione enchants a list of members so anyone who betrays them has 'SNEAK' magically appear on their face — Marietta Edgecombe gets the curse when she reports them.

question: Sirius Black dies in Order of the Phoenix during the Battle of the Department of Mysteries, killed by his cousin Bellatrix Lestrange. He falls backward through an ancient stone archway draped with a tattered veil. What's the in-universe name for this artifact in the Death Chamber?
answer: The Veil of Death (or simply 'the Veil')
choices: The Veil of Death (or simply 'the Veil')
context: The Veil is studied by the Department of Mysteries; characters report hearing voices from behind it. Whether the dead can be reached has been a source of fan theorizing for decades. Sirius's last words before he falls: 'Nice one, James!' — to Harry, who looks just like his father.

question: Half-Blood Prince (book 6, 2005) reveals that Voldemort split his soul into seven pieces to achieve immortality. What's the technical wizarding term for each of the soul-fragment containers?
context: Creating a Horcrux requires committing murder, the act that splits the soul. Horace Slughorn, the new Potions Master, explains the concept to a young Tom Riddle decades earlier — a memory Harry retrieves with Dumbledore's help. The book's title 'Half-Blood Prince' refers to Snape, whose mother Eileen was a Prince and father Tobias was a Muggle.

question: In Deathly Hallows (book 7, 2007), three legendary magical artifacts are introduced — gifts to three brothers from Death himself in the wizarding fairy tale 'The Tale of the Three Brothers.' They are the Cloak of Invisibility, the Resurrection Stone, and what wand?
context: The Elder Wand passes between owners by being mastered, not gifted — which is why Voldemort dies in the final book when the wand recognizes Harry as its true master via Draco's disarming of Dumbledore. Harry already owned the Cloak (a Potter family heirloom). The Resurrection Stone was hidden in Dumbledore's gift Snitch.

question: In the final Battle of Hogwarts in Deathly Hallows, one of the Weasley twins is killed by an exploding wall during the fighting in the corridor outside the Room of Requirement. Which twin dies?
context: Rowling has said she deliberated long over which twin to kill; she chose Fred because she felt readers would find it more shocking. Fred dies mid-laugh, having just made up with his estranged brother Percy. George survives and eventually marries Angelina Johnson, naming their first son Fred II.

question: Severus Snape's true loyalty is revealed in Deathly Hallows when Harry views his memories in the Pensieve. Snape had been in love with Lily Potter since childhood — protecting Harry for years out of devotion to her memory. What does Snape say in the memory, when Dumbledore asks if he still loves her after all these years?
context: The one-word answer 'Always' became one of the most quoted lines from the series, especially after Alan Rickman delivered it in the 2011 film. Snape's silver doe Patronus matches Lily's, confirming the depth of his love. Harry names his second son Albus Severus Potter in tribute.

question: Sirius Black, Remus Lupin, James Potter, and Peter Pettigrew were the four Marauders during their Hogwarts years. Each had an Animagus or transformation form named on the Marauder's Map. James was Prongs (a stag). What was Sirius's Animagus form?
answer: A large black dog (he was nicknamed Padfoot)
choices: A large black dog (he was nicknamed Padfoot)
A grey wolf (he was nicknamed Greybeard)
A black panther (he was nicknamed Shadowpaw)
A great horned owl (he was nicknamed Nightwing)
context: Remus Lupin was a werewolf — 'Moony' — but not an Animagus. James, Sirius, and Peter became unregistered Animagi during their Hogwarts years specifically to keep Lupin company during his monthly transformations. Peter's form was a rat — 'Wormtail' — and he hid as Ron's pet Scabbers for twelve years.

question: Hermione Granger pulls out a key item in Prisoner of Azkaban that explains how she's been attending two classes at the same time all year — a tiny golden necklace given to her by Professor McGonagall. What's it called?
context: The Ministry of Magic strictly regulates Time-Turners. Hermione uses hers to take extra classes including Ancient Runes and Muggle Studies. At the climax, she and Harry use it to rescue Buckbeak and Sirius. Rowling has admitted writing Time-Turners into the series was a mistake — it creates plot holes the rest of the books have to work around.

question: Newt Scamander's textbook Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them is referenced throughout the Harry Potter series. The Yule Ball in Goblet of Fire (book 4) features two student musicians performing — the in-universe wizarding rock band whose drummer wears a kilt. What's the band called?
context: Despite the name, the Weird Sisters are an all-male band (their name is a Macbeth reference). In the film, members were played by real musicians including Jarvis Cocker of Pulp and Jonny Greenwood of Radiohead. Pulp's Jarvis Cocker wrote and performed the band's original song 'Do the Hippogriff.'

question: Dolores Umbridge takes over Hogwarts in Order of the Phoenix as Headmistress and inquisitor. She's particularly cruel to Harry, forcing him to write 'I must not tell lies' with a quill that carves the words into the back of his hand. What does Hermione orchestrate to get Umbridge removed from the school?
answer: Tricking Umbridge into the Forbidden Forest where centaurs carry her off
choices: Tricking Umbridge into the Forbidden Forest where centaurs carry her off
Spiking her tea with Veritaserum to expose her Ministry blackmail
Convincing Peeves to flood her office with permanent corridors
Setting Hagrid's Blast-Ended Skrewts loose in her classroom
context: Umbridge had insulted centaurs as 'filthy half-breeds.' Firenze and his herd capture her after Hermione lures her in claiming Dumbledore has a hidden weapon there. Umbridge appears again in Deathly Hallows persecuting Muggle-borns at the Ministry; Harry punches her to retrieve Slytherin's locket from her.

question: Captain America: The First Avenger (2011) was directed by Joe Johnston and set during World War II. Steve Rogers receives a super-soldier serum in Brooklyn at a secret lab. What's the doctor's name who creates the serum and is killed by a Hydra assassin shortly after the procedure?
context: Stanley Tucci played Erskine. The serum's formula dies with him — which is why Hulk (gamma) and Iron Man (technology) become the closest other 'super' Avengers. Erskine had previously experimented on Johann Schmidt (the Red Skull) with an imperfect version that left Schmidt deformed. The serum amplifies a man's character.

question: Marvel's The Avengers (2012), directed by Joss Whedon, climaxes with the Battle of New York — the Chitauri attack through a portal over Stark Tower. The portal is opened by which Asgardian artifact, secretly the Mind Stone in disguise, in Loki's hands?
answer: Loki's scepter (containing the Mind Stone, with the Tesseract powering the portal)
choices: Loki's scepter (containing the Mind Stone, with the Tesseract powering the portal)
The Casket of Ancient Winters, repurposed by Frost Giants
The Eye of Agamotto, stolen from Kamar-Taj before Doctor Strange
The Reality Stone, infused in Mjolnir's hilt
context: The Tesseract is the Space Stone in disguise (revealed in later films). Loki's scepter contains the Mind Stone, which is later extracted to power Vision. Tony Stark's iconic 'I have a nuclear missile' redirect at the end — flying it through the closing portal — establishes his arc toward sacrifice.

question: Guardians of the Galaxy (2014) introduced a tree-like creature whose vocabulary consists almost entirely of three words. He's voiced by Vin Diesel and rebuilt as a sapling at film's end after a self-sacrifice. What's the character's name?
context: Groot first appeared in Marvel Tales #13 (November 1960) as a one-off alien menace. Diesel records 'I am Groot' in dozens of languages. The character's sacrifice at the end of GotG — 'We are Groot' — was scripted by James Gunn specifically to subvert expectations of disposable comic-relief sidekicks.

question: Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015) introduced two new heroes from Sokovia — siblings who were experimented on with the Mind Stone by Baron Strucker. Their character names in the comics are Wanda and Pietro Maximoff. What were the names used in Age of Ultron's promotional materials, to avoid X-Men rights confusion with Fox?
context: Marvel had a complicated rights situation with Fox's X-Men franchise. Fox could call them 'mutants'; Marvel could not. Fox's X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014) also featured Quicksilver, played by Evan Peters. Aaron Taylor-Johnson played Quicksilver in Age of Ultron; the character dies saving Hawkeye and a Sokovian child.

question: Captain America: Civil War (2016) features the first MCU appearance of Black Panther and Spider-Man (Tom Holland). The Russos' film climaxes at Berlin Airport with a massive 'team Cap vs team Iron Man' battle and then a private fight in Siberia. What does Tony learn there that destroys his alliance with Cap?
answer: Bucky (the Winter Soldier) murdered Tony's parents on Hydra's orders in 1991
choices: Bucky (the Winter Soldier) murdered Tony's parents on Hydra's orders in 1991
Cap knew about Bucky's brainwashing from 1948 and never told Tony
Zemo was actually Loki's variant and brokered the entire Sokovia Accords
S.H.I.E.L.D. had killed Tony's father to seize the Howling Commandos' files
context: Helmut Zemo (Daniel Brühl) engineers the entire Civil War from grief over his Sokovian family's death in Age of Ultron. The 1991 footage of Bucky killing Howard and Maria Stark is from Hydra's archives; Zemo's whole plan is to make Tony see it in Cap's presence. Civil War's last shot — Cap dropping his shield — frames Endgame's final reconciliation.

question: Doctor Strange (2016) was directed by Scott Derrickson and starred Benedict Cumberbatch as the arrogant neurosurgeon turned Sorcerer Supreme. What's the relic that protects Strange's hands — useless after the car accident that ends his surgical career, then crucial to his magical practice?
context: Cumberbatch broke his vocal cords during training. The Cloak of Levitation is sentient and chooses Strange in the climactic Kamar-Taj fight. Strange's signature relic the Eye of Agamotto contains the Time Stone — used to trap Dormammu in a bargaining loop in the film's climax: 'Dormammu, I've come to bargain.'

question: Black Panther (2018), directed by Ryan Coogler, takes place largely in Wakanda after T'Challa's father T'Chaka is killed (at the start of Civil War). The film's villain Erik Killmonger turns out to be T'Challa's American cousin, son of an exiled Wakandan prince. Who played him?
context: Coogler had previously directed Jordan in Fruitvale Station (2013) and Creed (2015). Killmonger's name Erik 'Killmonger' Stevens grew up in Oakland, the same city where Coogler grew up and where the Black Panther Party was founded in 1966. Killmonger's death line — 'Bury me in the ocean with my ancestors that jumped from ships' — is one of the most-quoted MCU lines.

question: Avengers: Endgame (2019) features the Avengers staging a 'time heist' to retrieve the six Infinity Stones from various points in their MCU history. In the heist, Black Widow and Hawkeye both volunteer to die on Vormir for the Soul Stone. Who actually makes the sacrifice?
choices: Both at once (the Red Skull permitting two souls)
Neither (they trick the Stone into accepting Loki's earlier death)
context: Natasha and Clint struggle for who gets to make the sacrifice — both believing themselves more expendable. Natasha wins the fight and falls. Scarlett Johansson had filmed her own death scene; the character was given a posthumous Black Widow film (2021). Endgame doesn't include a funeral for her, though Hawkeye laments her loss throughout the post-snap scenes.

question: Bob Kane took sole credit for Batman from 1939 through his death in 1998, signing his name on every cover and licensing deal. The other co-creator wrote the first Batman story, designed the cowl-and-cape look that replaced Kane's original red-and-yellow ski-mask sketches, named Bruce Wayne, came up with Commissioner Gordon, and introduced the secret-identity orphan backstory. DC formally added his credit to all Batman material in 2015, decades after his death in 1974. Who was this co-creator?
context: Finger died penniless in his Manhattan apartment in January 1974. Jerry Robinson, an artist on early Batman, had created the Joker; Robinson spent decades publicly campaigning for Finger's recognition. The 2017 documentary Batman & Bill traces the long fight by Finger's family and Marc Tyler Nobleman to get the credit added.

question: In 1986, Frank Miller's Daredevil 'Born Again' arc featured the Kingpin (Wilson Fisk) systematically destroying Matt Murdock's life — leaking his identity to the press, freezing his finances, demolishing his apartment building. The pivotal moment in the run is Murdock recovering in his mother's care, where Miller reveals that Matt's long-believed-dead mother is actually a nun under what name?
context: Born Again ran in Daredevil #227–233 with David Mazzucchelli on art. The story is widely considered one of the greatest superhero narratives ever published. The Netflix Daredevil show (2015–18) drew heavily from this run; Joanne Whalley played Sister Maggie in season three. Miller and Mazzucchelli followed Born Again with Batman: Year One in 1987.

question: Alan Moore's Watchmen (1986–87) was originally pitched to DC using a different set of characters — heroes DC had recently acquired from a defunct rival publisher, including The Question, Captain Atom, Blue Beetle, and Nightshade. DC editorial blocked Moore from using them because they wanted to actively publish those heroes in their own books. So Moore created analogs. Which Charlton hero was the inspiration for Rorschach?
context: Rorschach is Moore's deconstruction of The Question, a Steve Ditko hero who shared Ditko's Randian objectivist outlook. Dr. Manhattan is Captain Atom; Nite Owl is Blue Beetle; The Comedian is Peacemaker; Silk Spectre is Nightshade; Ozymandias is Thunderbolt. DC's Charlton heroes were rolled into the post-Crisis DC universe in 1986. Watchmen ran for 12 issues, September 1986 to October 1987.

question: Neil Gaiman wrote The Sandman from 1989 to 1996 across 75 monthly issues. Issue #19 — 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' — featured Dream contracting William Shakespeare's company to perform the play before its fairy subjects, in 1593 (the year of its presumed first performance). The issue made Gaiman the first comics writer ever to win what major literary prize?
answer: The World Fantasy Award for Short Fiction (1991)
choices: The World Fantasy Award for Short Fiction (1991)
The Hugo Award for Best Short Story (1991)
The Nebula Award for Best Novelette (1991)
context: The World Fantasy Convention amended its rules after the win, banning comic-book stories from future consideration. Gaiman was 30 at the time. Charles Vess illustrated the issue, drawing on classical fairy iconography for Titania and Oberon. The issue's premise — that Dream commissioned Shakespeare to write multiple plays in exchange for talent — remains one of the most-cited single comics ever produced.

question: Mark Millar wrote Kick-Ass in 2008, drawn by John Romita Jr., about a Brooklyn teenager who becomes a real-life costumed vigilante despite having no powers. The 2010 Matthew Vaughn film adaptation made an 11-year-old actress a star for playing a small foul-mouthed knife-wielding murder-vigilante in a purple wig. What was the character's name?
context: Chloë Grace Moretz played Hit-Girl at age 11. Her father Big Daddy was played by Nicolas Cage in full Adam West Batman voice. The 'C-word' scene caused a media firestorm; Roger Ebert wrote that he was 'morally outraged' by the film. Mark Millar's original comic ran for eight issues in 2008–09 from Marvel's Icon imprint.

question: The 1993 Batman: Knightfall storyline ran across 19 issues over six months and famously broke Batman's back. The breaking takes place in Batman #497 (July 1993) at the hands of a hulking villain genetically enhanced by a steroid called Venom. The villain was created by Doug Moench and Chuck Dixon expressly to defeat Batman. What's his name?
context: Bane is born in the fictional Caribbean prison of Peña Duro. He's intelligent — speaks multiple languages, a chess master — as well as physically overwhelming. Tom Hardy played him in The Dark Knight Rises (2012); Robert Swenson played him in Batman & Robin (1997). After breaking Batman, Jean-Paul Valley takes over the cowl as Azrael-Batman in a brutal, gun-using mode for over a year.

question: Garth Ennis and John McCrea's 1990s DC/Vertigo comic Hitman ran for 60 issues (1996–2001) starring a gun-for-hire who could read minds and see through walls because of an alien parasite incident. The character was named after a famous American film starring Sylvester Stallone. What's the character's name?
context: Tommy was a Gotham-set hitman, originally introduced in a Bloodlines crossover annual in 1993. The series is famous for issue #34, 'Of Thee I Sing,' a heartfelt Superman story where Tommy meets Supes on a rooftop. Ennis cited the issue as one of his proudest moments. Tommy dies in the final issue (#60) in a deliberately downbeat ending.

question: Brian Michael Bendis's Ultimate Spider-Man, launched in 2000, rebooted Spider-Man for a new audience with Mark Bagley on art. The series ran for 200+ issues with Bendis as sole writer. In 2011's Ultimate Comics: Spider-Man, Bendis introduced a Black Latino teenager who takes over the Spider-Man mantle after Peter Parker's Ultimate-universe death. What's the new Spider-Man's name?
context: Miles debuted in Ultimate Fallout #4 (August 2011). Sara Pichelli co-created him with Bendis. He became the lead character of the 2018 animated film Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, voiced by Shameik Moore. Miles's signature ability is a 'venom blast' bio-electric shock, which Peter Parker's Spider-Man can't do. His uncle Aaron Davis is also the Prowler.

question: Brian Azzarello and Eduardo Risso's 100 Bullets ran 100 issues (1999–2009) at Vertigo. The premise: Agent Graves approaches people who've been wronged and offers them an attaché case containing a gun, 100 untraceable bullets, and a folder identifying their tormentor. Graves represents the secret organization that has historically controlled American crime through 13 organized-crime families. What's the organization called?
context: The Trust is presented as the founding investors of America — 13 European families that funded the colonial expansion in exchange for ongoing dominance of American organized crime. The Minutemen are their enforcement arm; Graves is their former leader. The series won an Eisner for Best Continuing Series. Eduardo Risso's noir-influenced shadow-heavy artwork is considered some of the best in the medium.

question: Bill Watterson's Calvin and Hobbes ran for ten years (November 1985 to December 1995) at Universal Press Syndicate. The strip's six-year-old protagonist and his stuffed tiger Hobbes appeared in 3,160 strips. Watterson is famous in syndicated-comics history for what he refused to do across the run, costing him an estimated $300–400 million in revenue. What did he refuse?
answer: License the characters for merchandise (no plush Hobbes, no shirts, no commercials)
choices: License the characters for merchandise (no plush Hobbes, no shirts, no commercials)
Allow Sunday strips to expand beyond the standard four-panel grid
Permit foreign-language translations after the 1991 Italian incident
Hand off the strip to a successor cartoonist after his 1989 sabbatical
context: Watterson believed licensing would cheapen the strip — Hobbes had to remain ambiguous (real tiger? stuffed toy?), which was impossible if you could buy a plush. Charles Schulz had given different advice (Peanuts merchandising made Schulz hundreds of millions). The ubiquitous Calvin-peeing decals on pickup trucks are all unlicensed, illegal bootlegs.

question: Hergé's Tintin comics ran from 1929 to 1976 (with the unfinished Tintin and Alph-Art posthumous in 1986). The Belgian cartoonist's real name was Georges Remi; 'Hergé' comes from reading his initials R.G. in French. The series features Tintin's white fox terrier whose name in the original French is 'Milou.' What was the dog's name in English translations?
context: Hergé's Tintin has been translated into 70+ languages and sold over 200 million copies worldwide. The character's iconic cowlick, red plus-fours, and blue sweater were finalized by 1934. Steven Spielberg directed the 2011 motion-capture film The Adventures of Tintin starring Jamie Bell. Hergé took some hits postwar for collaborationist Belgian newspaper Le Soir publication under Nazi occupation.

question: Berkeley Breathed's Bloom County ran in syndication from 1980 to 1989, won a Pulitzer in 1987, and featured an array of bizarre characters in a fictional Midwestern town. Two characters became cultural icons: Opus the meditative penguin, and what cigar-chomping cat character so heavily marketed Breathed reportedly grew to hate him?
context: Breathed designed Bill specifically to mock Garfield's commercialization. The 'Ack! Thbbft!' catchphrase appeared on millions of T-shirts and mugs. Bill once ran for president in 1984 and 1988 on the Meadow Party ticket. Breathed walked away from Bloom County in 1989, did Outland (1989–1995) and Opus (2003–2008), then revived Bloom County on Facebook in 2015.

question: JK Rowling famously sketched out the seven-book Harry Potter plan on a napkin in 1990 during a delayed Manchester-to-London train ride. She spent five years developing it before writing began. The first publisher to accept Philosopher's Stone after rejection from twelve houses was a small London independent. Their initial print run was just 500 hardcover copies. Which publisher took the gamble?
context: Nigel Newton, Bloomsbury's chair, had his eight-year-old daughter Alice Newton read the opening chapter — she demanded the rest of the manuscript and refused to be put off. Bloomsbury offered Rowling £2,500 advance. Scholastic later acquired US rights for $105,000 — a then-record for a children's book. Today, surviving first-edition Bloomsbury hardcovers sell for $20,000–$50,000.

question: The Mirror of Erised, first encountered by Harry in Philosopher's Stone (book 1, 1997), shows the viewer their deepest, most desperate desire. The inscription on its frame reads 'Erised stra ehru oyt ube cafru oyt on wohsi' — a mirror-reversed sentence. What does the English original say?
answer: I show not your face but your heart's desire
choices: I show not your face but your heart's desire
Mirror of dreams, show me my heart's hidden joy
Within these depths a wish is granted unseen
What you seek the most you shall not find unspoken
context: 'Erised' is 'Desire' reversed. Dumbledore tells Harry: 'It does not do to dwell on dreams and forget to live.' The Philosopher's Stone is hidden inside the Mirror at the climax — only someone who wants to find the Stone but not use it can retrieve it. This is the test Harry passes and Quirrell/Voldemort fails.

question: Rowling deliberately based the four Hogwarts founders on the four classical elements and the four humors. Gryffindor (lion/red-gold) represents fire and courage. Slytherin (serpent/green-silver) represents water and ambition. Ravenclaw (eagle in books; raven in films) represents air and wit. What's Hufflepuff associated with, including its founder's signature heirloom?
answer: Earth, loyalty, and Helga Hufflepuff's gold-and-badger-engraved cup
choices: Earth, loyalty, and Helga Hufflepuff's gold-and-badger-engraved cup
Wood, patience, and Helga Hufflepuff's oak-and-honey-bee-engraved horn
Stone, kindness, and Helga Hufflepuff's silver-and-mole-engraved chalice
Mist, humility, and Helga Hufflepuff's pewter-and-fox-engraved goblet
context: The Cup is one of Voldemort's seven Horcruxes — stolen from Hepzibah Smith, an elderly heiress murdered by young Tom Riddle in the 1950s. Bellatrix Lestrange hides it in her vault at Gringotts; Harry, Ron, and Hermione break in during Deathly Hallows. Hufflepuff's badger symbol is a 'sett' (badger family group) — JK Rowling chose badgers in part because the Old English 'huff' means 'pant.'

question: Cedric Diggory's death in Goblet of Fire (2000) was a turning point — the first major character death in the series. The killing curse is delivered by Peter Pettigrew on Voldemort's command in a graveyard in Little Hangleton. Voldemort's revival in the same scene requires three ritual ingredients. The first is bone of the father, unknowingly taken. The second is flesh of the servant, willingly given (Wormtail's hand). What's the third?
answer: Blood of the enemy, forcibly taken (from Harry, with a silver dagger)
choices: Blood of the enemy, forcibly taken (from Harry, with a silver dagger)
Tear of the betrayer, freely shed (from Bellatrix, atop the cauldron)
Hair of the rival, secretly clipped (from Snape, during the gathering)
Tongue of the prophet, unwilling spoken (from Trelawney's grand-niece)
context: Voldemort uses Harry's blood because it carries Lily's protective magic. The act binds Harry and Voldemort more deeply — Harry survives Voldemort's killing curse in the Forest in Book 7 partly because Voldemort's body contains Harry's blood, anchoring Harry to life. Pettigrew sacrifices his own hand and Voldemort restores it as a silver hand of immense strength.

question: Mad-Eye Moody, the paranoid retired Auror who joins Hogwarts as Defense Against the Dark Arts professor in Goblet of Fire (book 4), turns out to be an imposter throughout the year — the real Moody locked in a magical trunk in his own office. Who was actually teaching the class under Polyjuice Potion?
context: Barty Crouch Jr. is a Death Eater whose Ministry-official father (Barty Crouch Sr.) had imprisoned him in the family home under the Imperius Curse after Azkaban. Voldemort frees him to engineer Harry's delivery to the graveyard. Brendan Gleeson played Moody; David Tennant played Crouch Jr. in the 2005 film. Crouch Jr. is later given the Dementor's Kiss by Cornelius Fudge, who refuses to believe Voldemort has returned.

question: In Order of the Phoenix (book 5), Dolores Umbridge takes over Hogwarts as 'High Inquisitor' on Cornelius Fudge's orders. Her cruel disciplinary methods include a magical detention quill that uses the writer's blood as ink, carving the words 'I must not tell lies' into the back of Harry's hand. The scar remains permanent on Harry's hand for the rest of the series. What 1996 author and political position is Umbridge consciously modeled on, per JK Rowling?
answer: A composite of authoritarian schoolteachers and middle-management bureaucrats Rowling had encountered
choices: A composite of authoritarian schoolteachers and middle-management bureaucrats Rowling had encountered
Margaret Thatcher's later-cabinet posture in the 1980s Education Ministry
Mary Whitehouse, the British media-decency campaigner of the 1970s and 80s
Enid Blyton's headmistress Miss Grayling from the Malory Towers series
context: Imelda Staunton played Umbridge in the 2007 film. Rowling has said Umbridge is her most-hated character in the series; she modeled her on a real-life teacher who 'bullied' Rowling's friend. The pink cardigan, the kitten plates, the saccharine voice — every detail is calibrated for maximum domestic-tyrant menace. Umbridge appears again in Deathly Hallows as a Ministry official under the Voldemort puppet regime.

question: Hogwarts has a poltergeist named Peeves who plagues students and even staff. Peeves answers to one and only one authority at the school besides Dumbledore — a particular old caretaker's predecessor. Filch hates Peeves. But the only one who can actually keep Peeves in line short of Dumbledore is who?
answer: The Bloody Baron (the Slytherin House ghost)
choices: The Bloody Baron (the Slytherin House ghost)
Nearly Headless Nick (the Gryffindor House ghost)
The Grey Lady (the Ravenclaw House ghost)
The Fat Friar (the Hufflepuff House ghost)
context: The Bloody Baron's bloodstains came from killing the Grey Lady (Helena Ravenclaw) in life — a backstory revealed in Deathly Hallows. Peeves was cut from all eight films. Rik Mayall (of The Young Ones) filmed scenes as Peeves for the first film, but all were ultimately cut by Chris Columbus. Mayall publicly groused about it for years.

question: In Deathly Hallows, Harry, Ron, and Hermione spend much of the book on the run, hunting Horcruxes while wearing Slytherin's locket Horcrux in turns. The locket exerts a corrupting psychological influence on its wearer. Harry, Ron, and Hermione each have different reactions. Ron's reaction in particular causes him to abandon Harry and Hermione for weeks before returning. What artifact does Ron use to find his way back to them?
answer: The Deluminator left to him by Dumbledore in his will
choices: The Deluminator left to him by Dumbledore in his will
A Howler from his mother delivered through Apparition
Hermione's enchanted DA Galleon she kept on her wrist
The Marauder's Map redirected through the Floo Network
context: The Deluminator (Dumbledore's silver cigarette-lighter device that absorbs light from a room) gains a special enchantment that lets Ron hear Hermione's voice and Apparate to her location when he speaks her name. Dumbledore had foreseen Ron's defection — Ron's three bequests in Dumbledore's will are the Deluminator (a tool to come back), the Sword of Gryffindor (for destroying Horcruxes), and the children's book The Tales of Beedle the Bard.

question: The Battle of Hogwarts in Deathly Hallows takes place on May 2, 1998 (a date Rowling has confirmed). Voldemort kills Snape in the Shrieking Shack to claim mastery of the Elder Wand. Voldemort believes Snape is the Wand's master because Snape killed Dumbledore. Why is Voldemort wrong about who really mastered the Elder Wand?
answer: Draco disarmed Dumbledore atop the Tower before Snape's curse, then Harry later disarmed Draco at Malfoy Manor
choices: Draco disarmed Dumbledore atop the Tower before Snape's curse, then Harry later disarmed Draco at Malfoy Manor
Dumbledore had quietly passed mastery to Aberforth in a sealed will days before the Tower confrontation
Snape's killing curse was a mercy killing that Dumbledore requested, which voids any wand-mastery transfer
Gellert Grindelwald never actually lost mastery of the Wand to Dumbledore back in their 1945 confrontation
context: The Elder Wand's mastery passes when its current owner is disarmed, not when killed. Draco's disarming of Dumbledore on the Astronomy Tower in Half-Blood Prince — moments before Snape's killing curse — quietly transferred mastery to Draco. Harry's later disarming of Draco at Malfoy Manor (Deathly Hallows) transferred it to Harry. When Voldemort fires the killing curse in the climactic duel, his own spell rebounds off the Wand and kills him.

question: JK Rowling has confirmed multiple deliberate dates throughout the series. Harry was born on July 31, 1980 (matching Rowling's own birthday). Voldemort attacked the Potters on Halloween — October 31, 1981 — killing James and Lily and giving Harry his lightning scar. The Potters were betrayed by their Secret-Keeper, switched at the last minute from Sirius to whom?
choices: Caradoc Dearborn (an early Order of the Phoenix member)
context: The Fidelius Charm hides a location/secret in a single chosen person; even those who already knew can no longer find it. Sirius convinced James and Lily that swapping him for the seemingly weak Peter would fool Voldemort. Peter immediately betrayed them. Sirius then went after Peter; Peter cut off his own finger, blew up a street, killed 12 Muggles, and transformed into Scabbers — leaving Sirius framed for the murders.

question: Iron Man (2008)'s third-act villain is Obadiah Stane, played by Jeff Bridges as the bald, bearded Stark Industries chairman who's been selling weapons to terrorists behind Tony's back. The character's comics counterpart appeared in 1982's Iron Man #163, created by Denny O'Neil and Luke McDonnell. What's the giant suit of armor Stane builds and dons for the film's climactic Stark Industries parking-lot fight?
context: Stane reverse-engineers the original Mark I suit Tony built in the cave. The Iron Monger is roughly twice Iron Man's size. Bridges shaved his head for the role; the bald look surprised audiences expecting his Big Lebowski-era hair. The film was 2008's third-highest-grossing US release behind The Dark Knight and Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull.

question: Joss Whedon's The Avengers (2012) opened to $207.4 million in its US opening weekend — at the time the biggest opening in cinema history. The film established Marvel's three-act team-up template. A famous one-shot circling tracking-shot during the Battle of New York shows each Avenger fighting Chitauri in sequence. Who closes the shot, leaping off a ruined taxi to fire a single arrow that destroys an oncoming Leviathan beast?
context: The tracking shot was extensively reshot in post-production to add the camera weave-and-pan, then finished in CGI. Jeremy Renner had been in the MCU since a Thor (2011) cameo but Avengers gave him his first major screen time. The cinematic 'one-shot Avengers showcase' became a recurring Marvel device repeated in Age of Ultron's opening and Endgame's portal sequence.

question: Iron Man 3 (2013) features the apparent return of Iron Man's long-foreshadowed comics archnemesis the Mandarin. The character was teased throughout the first two films via the Ten Rings terrorist group. In Iron Man 3, Ben Kingsley plays the Mandarin as a terrifying bin-Laden-styled mastermind. The mid-film twist is that Kingsley's Mandarin is actually what?
answer: A drug-addled British actor named Trevor Slattery, hired by the real villain to be a public face
choices: A drug-addled British actor named Trevor Slattery, hired by the real villain to be a public face
An AIM holographic projection driven from a hidden submarine docked off the Miami coastline
Aldrich Killian's hallucination created by the Extremis virus injected into Tony Stark's bloodstream
A shapeshifting Skrull infiltrator using a technology that would later be revealed in Captain Marvel
context: The real villain is Aldrich Killian (Guy Pearce), CEO of Advanced Idea Mechanics (AIM), who hired Slattery as the public face of the Mandarin while he experimented with the Extremis virus. Iron Man 3 was Shane Black's directorial entry into the MCU, his first feature since Kiss Kiss Bang Bang (2005). The film angered some comics fans furious about the Mandarin twist; a 2014 Marvel One-Shot (All Hail the King) walked back the implication that the 'real' Mandarin doesn't exist.

question: Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015) introduced the Vision, an android created from JARVIS's consciousness, an Infinity Stone, and a body Tony built with Bruce Banner using Helen Cho's regeneration cradle. The Mind Stone is placed in Vision's forehead. Vision proves himself worthy of Mjolnir by casually picking up the hammer at the film's party scene. Who plays Vision?
context: Bettany had voiced JARVIS (Tony's AI butler — 'Just A Rather Very Intelligent System') since 2008's Iron Man. The actor wore prosthetic-and-face-paint pink-and-green Vision makeup that took hours each day. Paul Bettany is married to actress Jennifer Connelly. The hammer-lifting scene was filmed but kept under wraps from the cast until released.

question: Avengers: Infinity War (2018) marked the end-act of Phase 3 with the Russos' first Avengers film. The film opens with Thanos killing Loki and Heimdall aboard the Asgardian refugee ship, then progressively collecting six Infinity Stones. The Soul Stone requires a soul-for-soul sacrifice on a remote planet called Vormir. Who does Thanos sacrifice?
answer: Gamora, his adopted daughter, by throwing her off a cliff
choices: Gamora, his adopted daughter, by throwing her off a cliff
Nebula, his adopted daughter, in a duel-to-the-death ritual
Ebony Maw, his most loyal Black Order servant, with a spell
Drax's daughter, returned to him through Ravager negotiations
context: Zoe Saldana played Gamora. Endgame later resurrects a 2014-era Gamora through the time heist. The Red Skull, banished from Earth by the Tesseract's Space Stone in Captain America: The First Avenger (1945), guards the Soul Stone on Vormir. Ross Marquand voices Red Skull (Hugo Weaving, who played him in 2011, declined). The 'soul for a soul' rule pays off again with Black Widow's Endgame sacrifice.

question: Captain Marvel (2019) is set primarily in 1995, before any of the other MCU films chronologically except parts of Captain America: The First Avenger. Brie Larson stars as Carol Danvers, a US Air Force pilot who gains photon-blast powers from the Tesseract's Space Stone. The film's chief twist concerns the Skrulls — the green shapeshifting aliens. What turns out to be true about them, contradicting comics canon?
answer: They are sympathetic refugees fleeing genocide, not the evil empire they appear to be, and the Kree are the true villains
choices: They are sympathetic refugees fleeing genocide, not the evil empire they appear to be, and the Kree are the true villains
They are revealed to be the source of all human mutation genes throughout history, retconning the X-Men's mutants
They are revealed to have created the Asgardians using genetic engineering, retconning the entire Bifrost system
They are revealed to be Phyla-Vell variants from another dimension entirely, brought through by Captain Mar-Vell
context: Ben Mendelsohn plays Talos, a Skrull refugee leader, with cheek-pouch prosthetics. The Kree — purple/blue antagonists in Guardians of the Galaxy and elsewhere — are framed as the genocidal imperialists. Jude Law plays Yon-Rogg, Carol's mentor-turned-traitor in the Kree Starforce. The de-aging tech used on Samuel L. Jackson for the 1995 Fury sequences was a milestone in MCU VFX.

question: Avengers: Endgame (2019)'s 'time heist' splits the surviving Avengers into teams traveling to specific points in the MCU's past. Captain America, Iron Man, Hulk, and Ant-Man travel to 2012 New York during the Battle for the Tesseract. Cap fights an alternate-timeline version of himself. The fight ends with the present-day Cap whispering two words that throw the past Cap off-guard. What does he say?
context: The 'Hail Hydra' line plays off a then-recent comics storyline (Secret Empire, 2017) where Captain America was retconned into a lifelong Hydra agent — a much-controversial Nick Spencer storyline. The Russos winked at the controversy. The line briefly stuns 2012 Cap (who at that point believed Bucky dead since 1945) long enough for present-Cap to win the elevator fight.

question: Tom Holland's Spider-Man debuted in Captain America: Civil War (2016) but got his first solo MCU film with Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017), directed by Jon Watts. The film's villain is a Brooklyn-based salvager who has been illicitly building tech from Battle of New York debris into a winged armored suit. Michael Keaton plays him. What's the character's comics name?
context: Keaton's casting was a meta-joke — he'd played Batman (1989, 1992) and the actor Birdman in the 2014 Best Picture winner Birdman, both winged characters. Adrian Toomes first appeared in Amazing Spider-Man #2 in 1963. Homecoming was a Sony-Marvel co-production made possible by the 2015 deal that put Spider-Man in the MCU after years of Sony's solo Andrew Garfield films flopping.

question: Action Comics #1 (April 1938) introduced Superman with a cover by Joe Shuster showing the Man of Steel lifting a green car over his head while terrified onlookers flee. The cover became one of the most-imitated images in comics history. The original cover painting was reportedly lost by DC's offices for decades, but Joe Shuster's original interior pencils for the issue did survive. A pristine CGC-graded 9.0 copy of Action Comics #1 sold at Heritage Auctions on April 4, 2024 for a record-shattering amount. What was the final price?
context: The previous record was $3.2 million for a 9.0 in 2021. Action Comics #1 had a print run of about 200,000; experts estimate fewer than 100 copies survive today in any condition. The cover price was 10 cents. Heritage Auctions's $6M was the highest-ever paid for a single comic book. The Vincent Zurzolo / Stephen Fishler company ComicConnect tracks pricing in detail.

question: Jack Kirby left Marvel for DC Comics in 1970 during a contentious dispute over creator credit and ownership. At DC he created an interconnected mythology of warring cosmic factions across four ongoing titles — Mister Miracle, Forever People, New Gods, and Jimmy Olsen — that didn't sell well at the time but would become some of the most-influential comics ever made. Two warring planets and their gods form the heart of the saga: Apokolips (ruled by Darkseid) and what counterpart paradise-world?
choices: Themyscira (ruled by Queen Hippolyta of the Amazons)
Olympus Major (ruled by Zeus of the New Olympians)
Krypton II (ruled by the survivors of the original Krypton)
context: Kirby's Fourth World saga ran 1970–73 at DC before all four titles were cancelled. Darkseid is the most enduring creation — a New York-accent space tyrant whose face is carved from blackened stone. He has been used as the primary cosmic villain in Crisis on Infinite Earths, Final Crisis (2008), and the Zack Snyder Justice League cut. Steppenwolf and the Parademons are also from this saga. Kirby returned to Marvel in 1976.

question: In December 1986, Marvel editor-in-chief Jim Shooter signed a deal with Universal Pictures for a live-action Galactus film. The deal collapsed when Shooter was fired in 1987 after a series of editorial disputes. One of the most-celebrated bridges built by Shooter during his tenure was a 1984 to 1985 maxi-series that pitted heroes against an alien Beyonder on a patchwork-planet called Battleworld. What was the series called, which became Marvel's first 'event' crossover and is widely credited with creating the modern comics-event template?
context: Mike Zeck and John Beatty drew the bulk of Secret Wars. The 12-issue series was tied directly to a Mattel toy line; Mattel had wanted a Marvel branded event to push action figures, the same toy-driven approach DC's Super Powers line was using. The Beyonder's appearance, a glowing white humanoid, wouldn't be revealed until issue 11. Spider-Man also got his black costume in Secret Wars, which later became Venom.

question: Steve Ditko walked away from Spider-Man after Amazing Spider-Man #38 (July 1966), reportedly without leaving a forwarding address. Ditko and Stan Lee had stopped speaking face-to-face for months before the departure — communicating only through editor Sol Brodsky. The dispute was reportedly over multiple issues including character direction, page rates, and Ditko's increasingly Randian objectivist views. Ditko never publicly discussed Spider-Man for the rest of his life. He died in his New York apartment in what year?
context: Ditko was 90 years old when he died on June 29, 2018. He was found two days later. He had lived a famously private life — refusing interviews, publishing essays only through small press. His objectivism led him to create Mr. A (1967), a black-and-white-morality character published outside Marvel. John Romita Sr. took over Spider-Man and softened the visual style. Ditko also co-created Doctor Strange (Strange Tales #110, 1963).

question: Alan Moore's Watchmen ran 12 issues from September 1986 to October 1987. Issue #5, 'Fearful Symmetry,' is famous for being structured as a literal mirror — the panels in the first half of the issue are reflected by the second half, with the centerfold (pages 14–15) being the visual fulcrum. Each page mirrors its opposite. The chapter title comes from a William Blake poem. What's the poem called?
context: The opening lines: 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night; / What immortal hand or eye, / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?' Each Watchmen issue closes with a literary epigraph from sources including Nietzsche, Genesis, Einstein, Carl Jung, and Bob Dylan. Moore is famously meticulous about issue construction; he wrote full prose-style scripts running 40+ pages per issue for Dave Gibbons.

question: Neil Gaiman's Sandman issue #50 (June 1993), titled 'Ramadan,' is a self-contained story about Haroun al-Rashid, the 8th-century Abbasid caliph of Baghdad. Al-Rashid summons Dream to make a bargain: in exchange for Dream's protection, he will preserve the golden age of Baghdad forever in a sealed bottle. The story addresses real grief over the modern destruction of the city. P. Craig Russell drew the issue in a deliberately illuminated-manuscript style. The story made its print debut at what is widely seen to be a politically tragic moment. What was happening at the time?
answer: The first months after the 1991 Gulf War and the 1990s Iraq sanctions regime were intensifying
choices: The first months after the 1991 Gulf War and the 1990s Iraq sanctions regime were intensifying
The 1979 Iranian Revolution had toppled the Shah and stranded American hostages in Tehran
The 1982 Israeli action in Lebanon was destroying Beirut's reputation as Paris of the East
The 1986 Chernobyl disaster had displaced Eastern European writers across multiple cultures
context: Sandman #50 sold significantly above its usual run — many comics shops cited it as a 'lifetime favorite' single issue.
