Gaiman has spoken about the personal grief he had over reports of Baghdad's modern destruction; the issue's ending, where Dream tells the story to a small boy crouching against a wall in modern Baghdad, has become a much-shared image among Iraqi diaspora writers. P. Craig Russell would later adapt The Sandman into multiple opera librettos.

question: Mike Mignola's Hellboy #1 (March 1994) was published by Dark Horse Comics after Mignola left Marvel and DC, where he had been a high-profile interior artist for over a decade. Hellboy was conceived as a 1994 Comic-Con sketch Mignola did during downtime. The character's full name — given by Trevor Bruttenholm — is a riff on a Bavarian demon-name. What is Hellboy's actual birth-name in the comics' mythos?
context: Anung Un Rama means 'and upon his brow is set a crown of flame.' Hellboy's destiny in the comics is to bring about the end of days — the Right Hand of Doom (his oversized stone right hand) is the literal key to releasing the seven Dragon-gods of the Ogdru Hem. Mignola revealed Hellboy's true heritage gradually over decades. Ron Perlman played him in the 2004 and 2008 del Toro films; David Harbour did the 2019 reboot. Mignola's spare brushwork was directly influenced by Mike Kaluta and Bernie Wrightson.

question: Garth Ennis's Punisher MAX run (2004–2008, Marvel's adult imprint MAX) ran 60 issues drawn primarily by Leandro Fernandez and Goran Parlov. The opening arc 'In the Beginning' (issues 1–6) sees an aged Frank Castle hunting down the Punisher's original 1976 villain, who had emerged as a Maltese Mafia don. Who was Frank tracking — the killer of Frank's wife and children in Central Park in 1976?
answer: The Gnucci family, then back to Bruno Costa and ultimately the original Costa hit team
choices: The Gnucci family, then back to Bruno Costa and ultimately the original Costa hit team
Jigsaw (Billy Russo) operating out of the Hudson Hospital ICU ward
The Kingpin in his Hell's Kitchen real-estate office on the 25th floor
Barracuda's old crew including the original Microchip from Cape May
context: Ennis's Punisher MAX is widely considered the definitive take on the character — Frank as a hollowed-out Vietnam vet, the mob as petty cruel men, no redemption. The Frank Castle Sr. flashbacks were drawn with deliberate visual flatness compared to the gritty present-day scenes. Tim Bradstreet did most of the painted MAX covers. Ennis followed up with The Punisher: Born (2003, with Darick Robertson) about Frank in Vietnam.

question: Ed Brubaker and Steve Epting's 2005 Captain America Winter Soldier arc revealed that Bucky Barnes had survived his apparent 1945 death — recovered by the Soviets, given a bionic arm, and cryogenically frozen between assignments as their top assassin. The first issue showing the modern Winter Soldier reveal was Captain America (Vol. 5) #11. Brubaker had to convince Marvel editor-in-chief Joe Quesada to allow Bucky's resurrection — Quesada had famously declared that only three deaths in comics should stay permanent. Which three?
answer: Uncle Ben, Jason Todd, and Bucky Barnes himself
choices: Uncle Ben, Jason Todd, and Bucky Barnes himself
Uncle Ben, Gwen Stacy, and Tony Stark Sr. (Howard Stark)
Aunt May, Jason Todd, and the original Captain Marvel (Mar-Vell)
Doctor Strange's mentor, Jean Grey, and Bucky Barnes himself
context: Brubaker's pitch focused on Bucky as a tortured agent kept frozen between hits — emphasizing his lost humanity rather than reversing the death cheaply. Quesada approved. Jason Todd would later be brought back in 2005 via Judd Winick's Under the Red Hood arc; Uncle Ben has stayed dead but appeared in Spider-Verse alternate-realities. Brubaker continued his Cap run through 2012 with Marcos Martin, Mike Perkins, and Butch Guice. The Winter Soldier arc was adapted as the 2014 Russo Brothers film.

question: Bone, Jeff Smith's self-published 55-issue series (1991–2004), tells the story of three cousins exiled from the town of Boneville after a Phoney Bone scheme goes wrong. They find themselves in a sword-and-sorcery valley where they encounter a young woman named Thorn. Thorn's grandmother is the elderly Gran'ma Ben, who turns out to be the deposed queen of the valley. What was Gran'ma Ben's real name as queen?
context: Gran'ma Ben's daughter Briar Harvestar is the saga's villain — sister-turned-Lord of the Locusts. Jeff Smith published the entire series himself through Cartoon Books, refusing offers from Marvel and DC. The full series is 1,332 pages. Scholastic released the entire run in 9 color volumes from 2005–2009, exposing a generation of younger readers to the saga. Smith followed up with RASL (2008–12) and the 2018 Tüki: Save the Humans series.

question: Frank Miller and Lynn Varley's 1989 Daredevil: Love and War one-shot (an oversized hardcover) introduced Vanessa Fisk as the kidnapped wife of the Kingpin. Miller's 1986 Born Again arc had established Vanessa as the only thing softening the Kingpin's heart. Love and War follows a deranged scientist named Victor who has kidnapped Vanessa, while the Kingpin captures Victor's wife to extort her return. The book is famous for its lush painted color art by Varley. What other late-1980s Miller collaboration did Varley provide painted color for?
choices: Sin City: The Hard Goodbye (1991) and Sin City: A Dame to Kill For (1993)
Elektra: Assassin (1986) with Bill Sienkiewicz and Ronin (1983)
Daredevil: Man Without Fear (1993) and Batman: Year One (1987)
context: Lynn Varley was Miller's wife from 1980–2005. Her painted color work was a major departure from comics' usual flat-color print processes; The Dark Knight Returns featured halftone gradients and Sun Yat-Sen yellow flecks that gave Gotham an apocalyptic warmth. Varley also colored Miller's Ronin (1983), Elektra Lives Again (1990), and 300 (1998). Varley and Miller divorced in 2005 after Miller's All-Star Batman & Robin began.

question: DC Comics's Crisis on Infinite Earths (April 1985 to March 1986) ran 12 issues, drawn entirely by George Pérez. The series consolidated DC's tangled parallel-Earth continuity into a single universe and killed dozens of legacy characters. Pérez personally drew over 1,200 pages. The maxi-series's most-iconic single image — used on Crisis #7's cover (October 1985) — depicts Superman cradling a fallen character whose face is in shadow. That cover image has been repeatedly homaged in DC comics for forty years. Who is Superman cradling?
choices: Lois Lane in her Earth-2 incarnation
context: Supergirl dies in Crisis #7 attacking the Anti-Monitor on his throneworld. Pérez's cover composition — Superman in mid-cry, holding the broken body — was inspired by a Pieta motif (the Madonna cradling the dead Christ). Pérez told interviewers he drew the cover at his kitchen table the morning after his mother had passed away. The cover has been parodied in The Simpsons, Family Guy, multiple anniversary covers, and Justice League: Earth 2 (2002). Kara would not return to the main DC continuity until 2004.

question: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone was rejected by twelve publishers before Bloomsbury accepted it in 1996. JK Rowling has named several of the rejecting publishers in interviews over the years. The first major US-rights bid came from Arthur A. Levine Books, an imprint of Scholastic, at the 1997 Bologna Children's Book Fair. The advance Scholastic paid Rowling was the highest amount ever paid for a children's book at that point. What was the advance?
context: The Bloomsbury UK advance was £2,500 — about $4,000 USD at the time. The Scholastic deal in spring 1997 was specifically to publish under the new 'Arthur A. Levine Books' imprint. Levine had to convince Scholastic's board on the gamble; he flew to Frankfurt in October 1996 to read the manuscript over a weekend. Levine personally edited the first several books and named the imprint after himself. He retired in 2019; the imprint was folded.

question: The seven Horcruxes in Voldemort's plan, in canonical order created, are: (1) Tom Riddle's diary [destroyed in Chamber of Secrets]; (2) Marvolo Gaunt's ring [destroyed by Dumbledore in 1996]; (3) Salazar Slytherin's locket [destroyed in Deathly Hallows]; (4) Helga Hufflepuff's cup [destroyed in Deathly Hallows]; (5) Rowena Ravenclaw's diadem [destroyed in Deathly Hallows]; (6) Voldemort's snake Nagini [destroyed in Deathly Hallows]; (7) Harry Potter himself [destroyed in Forbidden Forest]. What specific weapon does Ron Weasley use to destroy Hufflepuff's cup in Deathly Hallows?
answer: A basilisk fang from the Chamber of Secrets
choices: A basilisk fang from the Chamber of Secrets
Godric Gryffindor's Sword pulled from the Sorting Hat
Fiendfyre conjured by Vincent Crabbe in the Room of Requirement
Ravenclaw's Diadem-shard fragment of Voldemort's split soul
context: Hermione retrieves the basilisk fangs in Deathly Hallows from the Chamber of Secrets — she'd memorized the way after Ron 'opens' it by mimicking Parseltongue. Each Horcrux requires a specific weapon-or-poison powerful enough to overcome the dark magic. The Sword of Gryffindor (impregnated with basilisk venom from Harry's stabbing it in Chamber of Secrets) destroys the locket. Fiendfyre destroys the Diadem (Crabbe's curse going out of control). Neville destroys Nagini with the Sword.

question: In Half-Blood Prince (book 6, 2005), Harry obtains a used Potions textbook with marginal annotations from a previous owner. The annotations dramatically improve every potion Harry brews. The previous owner had also invented original spells written in the book — including 'Sectumsempra,' a slashing curse Harry uses against Draco Malfoy in a bathroom duel that nearly kills him. The book is signed 'Property of the Half-Blood Prince.' Whose book was it?
answer: Severus Snape (his mother was Eileen Prince)
choices: Severus Snape (his mother was Eileen Prince)
Sirius Black (his mother was a 'prince' in family fiction)
Tom Riddle (a Slytherin Prefect during his Hogwarts years)
Regulus Black (a young man called R.A.B. in Sirius's letters)
context: Snape's father Tobias was a Muggle; his mother Eileen Prince was a pure-blood witch. 'Half-Blood Prince' is Snape's invented self-styled title, combining his mother's surname and his mixed heritage. The book is buried in Snape's adolescent diary-prose handwriting. Harry hides the book in the Room of Requirement at the end of Book 6. Rowling has admitted the book's reveal felt thinner than she wanted — many readers had figured out Snape was the Prince by issue #1's mid-publication speculation.

question: The Order of the Phoenix (book 5, 2003) headquarters is 12 Grimmauld Place, the ancestral London townhouse of the Black family. Sirius's nightmarish childhood home is filled with Black family tapestries, dark-arts artifacts, and the portrait of his portrait-shrieking mother Walburga Black. The house is protected by the Fidelius Charm with Dumbledore as Secret-Keeper. The house elf attached to the property is a disgruntled, generations-old half-mad servant who at first betrays the Order before reconciling with the protagonists. What's the elf's name?
context: Kreacher's loyalty to the Black family — particularly to Sirius's brother Regulus — explains his initial bitterness toward Sirius (who detested the family). Regulus had been a Death Eater before turning on Voldemort and retrieving the locket-Horcrux; Regulus took Kreacher into the cave-trap with Voldemort and ordered Kreacher to retrieve the locket. Kreacher kept Regulus's secret for years until Harry, Ron, and Hermione earn his trust in Deathly Hallows. The earlier book introduced Dobby and Winky.

question: The Forbidden Forest at Hogwarts is home to several supernatural creature populations — centaurs in the deeper wood, acromantulas (giant intelligent spiders) in colonies deeper still. Aragog, the spider patriarch and acromantula colony founder, is the spider Hagrid raised as a student in 1942. Aragog dies in Half-Blood Prince of natural causes. What does Hagrid request Harry and Ron's help with for Aragog's funeral, which leads to a critical Slughorn-memory retrieval moment?
answer: Lifting the body to bury it (Aragog is the size of a small elephant)
choices: Lifting the body to bury it (Aragog is the size of a small elephant)
Brewing a memorial potion using Aragog's venom for the funeral guests
Distracting Mosag and the offspring spiders during the burial ceremony
Translating Latin funerary phrases Hagrid had memorized for the eulogy
context: Slughorn becomes drunk on Hagrid's homemade wine at the funeral, which is when Harry uses Felix Felicis (Liquid Luck) to extract the unaltered Horcrux memory from him. Aragog had been Hagrid's secret 'pet' since his Hogwarts expulsion in 1943 — when Tom Riddle framed Hagrid for Aragog's release. Rubeus Hagrid is half-giant — his mother Fridwulfa was a giantess; his father was a wizard. Robbie Coltrane played Hagrid in all eight films.

question: Harry Potter's wand contains a phoenix tail feather from Dumbledore's bird Fawkes — the same source feather that's in Voldemort's wand. This 'brother wand' connection causes the Priori Incantatem (golden cage of light) effect when Harry and Voldemort directly attack each other in the Goblet of Fire graveyard scene. The Priori Incantatem wand-effect was created by Olivander, the legendary wandmaker. What's Mr. Olivander's first name?
context: Mr. Ollivander runs Ollivanders, the wand shop at 1 Diagon Alley, founded 382 BC. He's the leading wand expert in wizarding Britain. The phoenix-feather brother wands ('twin cores') are unusually rare; only Fawkes ever donated feathers to wandmakers. Voldemort kidnaps Mr. Ollivander early in Deathly Hallows seeking knowledge of wand mastery, leading Voldemort to track down the Elder Wand. John Hurt played Ollivander in films 1 and 7-8. The shop's signature line: 'The wand chooses the wizard.'

question: Hermione Granger's parents — both dentists in London — appear briefly in Chamber of Secrets and Goblet of Fire. In Deathly Hallows, Hermione casts a memory-charm on them and sends them off so they cannot be tortured for her location. She erases their memory of having a daughter and gives them new identities. What new names does she give them?
context: Hermione plants in her parents' minds the idea that they've always wanted to retire to Australia. She intends to find and restore them after the war. Rowling has stated in interviews that Hermione successfully reunites with her parents and restores their memories after Voldemort's fall. The Granger-parents subplot didn't make it into the film of Deathly Hallows. The scene where Hermione enchants the family photos to erase herself is one of the most emotional moments in the book.

question: The Marauders — James Potter, Sirius Black, Remus Lupin, Peter Pettigrew — became unregistered Animagi in their Hogwarts years (1971–1978) to keep Lupin company during his monthly werewolf transformations. Becoming an Animagus is described in the books as 'extraordinarily difficult magic' — requiring years of preparation. What plant must an Animagus hopeful keep a leaf of in their mouth for an entire month uninterrupted as part of the process?
answer: A leaf from the Mandrake plant
choices: A leaf from the Mandrake plant
A leaf from the Aconite plant (wolfsbane)
A leaf from the Belladonna plant (nightshade)
A leaf from the Mistletoe plant (Druidic origin)
context: If the leaf is dislodged before the full month, the wizard must start over. The full ritual involves further potion-brewing during a specific lightning storm. The Marauders accomplished the transformation in fifth year — about three years of work. McGonagall (registered Animagus, tabby cat) is the only known legal Animagus in the modern era. Rita Skeeter (beetle) is an unregistered Animagus exposed by Hermione in Goblet of Fire.

question: The Battle of Hogwarts ends with Voldemort firing the killing curse at Harry in the Great Hall — and the curse rebounding to kill Voldemort because Voldemort has been the unwitting master of his own death. Harry survives the prior killing curse in the Forest because of the soul-anchor effect of Voldemort containing Harry's blood. Harry's blood was taken in 1995 to revive Voldemort. The 'King's Cross' chapter between forest-death and Great Hall return features Harry in conversation with Dumbledore. What does Harry see lying under a bench during this dream-sequence?
answer: A flayed, child-sized creature that represents the broken remnant of Voldemort's soul
choices: A flayed, child-sized creature that represents the broken remnant of Voldemort's soul
A silver phoenix feather lying alongside a perfect green basilisk egg
A tarnished mirror reflecting the Forest of Dean's protective enchantments
A torn fragment of the Resurrection Stone wrapped in Harry's mother's handkerchief
context: The King's Cross dream-sequence is one of Rowling's most-debated chapters — whether Harry is dead, dreaming, in limbo, or somewhere else. The flayed creature represents the soul-fragment of Voldemort attached to Harry as the seventh Horcrux, now severed. Dumbledore's appearance allows him to explain the entire Hallows-and-Horcruxes plan to Harry. After the conversation, Harry chooses to return to life; the Forbidden Forest scene plays out with Voldemort believing he'd just killed Harry.

question: Iron Man (2008) was directed by Jon Favreau and made for $140 million on a film that had been in development hell since New Line Cinema acquired the rights in 1992. The film's casting was a public gamble; Robert Downey Jr. was uninsurable due to past drug arrests, and Marvel Studios had to pay for his insurance bond personally. The pivotal cave-escape scene was largely improvised by Downey and Jeff Bridges as Obadiah Stane. The film's opening sequence with the Stark Industries weapons convoy in Afghanistan ends with a now-iconic AC/DC song playing as Tony Stark gets into the lead Humvee. What's the song?
context: Favreau picked Back in Black to immediately signal Tony's rock-star personality. The film's score by Ramin Djawadi (later of Game of Thrones) features blues-rock guitar reminiscent of AC/DC throughout. The original cut had Iron Maiden's 'Iron Man' over the same scene, but rights issues forced the change. Stan Lee has a cameo as 'Hugh Hefner' at the Vegas charity event near the film's opening, mistaken by Tony for the real Hef.

question: Joss Whedon's The Avengers (2012) features one of the most-quoted lines in superhero film history during the Stuttgart cathedral scene: Loki commands a frightened crowd of gala-attendees to kneel, asking 'Is not this simpler? Is this not your natural state?' An elderly German man stands up alone in defiance. What's the line the old man delivers, alluding to a specific historical period?
answer: Not to men like you. — There are always men like you.
choices: Not to men like you. — There are always men like you.
We have been ruled by tyrants before. — We did not bend then.
I have stood in stadiums while men like you raved. — I will not bow now.
You speak with the voice of those we buried. — I do not kneel.
context: The implication is that the old man is a Holocaust survivor — a German Jew who lived through Nazi rule and refuses to bow to another would-be tyrant. The brief moment is one of the most emotionally-loaded in the film. Loki responds by attempting to kill him before Captain America's first major MCU heroic moment intervenes. Whedon wrote the German man's lines specifically to ground Loki's mid-film menace in real-world resonance.

question: The Russos' Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014) was inspired heavily by 1970s political-thriller films — particularly Alan J. Pakula's All the President's Men (1976), Three Days of the Condor (1975), and The Parallax View (1974). The Russos cast veteran actor Robert Redford as the senior S.H.I.E.L.D. official Alexander Pierce specifically because of his association with that era. What was Redford's iconic 1970s political-thriller role that directly informed the Pierce casting?
answer: Bob Woodward in All the President's Men (1976) and Joseph Turner in Three Days of the Condor

Sundance in Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969) and Jeremiah Johnson title role
Bill McKay in The Candidate (1972) and his Oscar role as Norman in Ordinary People
Hubbell Gardner in The Way We Were (1973) and Roy Hobbs in The Natural (1984)
context: Redford reportedly took the part for $1 to do something his grandchildren could see. Pierce is revealed to be a Hydra operative — Hydra having quietly subverted S.H.I.E.L.D. from within since 1945. The film's helicarrier-takedown finale (Cap leaping between three falling helicarriers) was practically choreographed before becoming CGI. Captain America: The Winter Soldier opened to $95M domestically and is widely cited as one of the best-reviewed Marvel films, sitting at 90% on Rotten Tomatoes.

question: Black Panther (2018) was directed by Ryan Coogler and shot largely at Pinewood Atlanta Studios. The film's Wakandan culture combined elements from real African nations — South Africa's Xhosa language is spoken in many scenes, with John Kani as T'Chaka teaching the language to the rest of the cast. The Dora Milaje (Wakanda's all-female bodyguard corps) are inspired by a real West African military tradition. Which historical force inspired them?
answer: The Agojie of the Kingdom of Dahomey, an all-female military regiment that existed from the 17th to the late 19th century
choices: The Agojie of the Kingdom of Dahomey, an all-female military regiment that existed from the 17th to the late 19th century
The Mino of the Zulu Kingdom under Shaka's reign in the early 19th century, before colonial dissolution
The Nubian Queens' Guard of ancient Meroe, which trained women warriors from the 5th century BC onward
The Carthaginian Women's Auxiliary that defended the city during the Third Punic War, 149-146 BC
context: The Agojie (also called 'Dahomey Amazons' by European writers) numbered up to 6,000 women at their peak. They were officially disbanded in 1894 after the French conquest of Dahomey. The 2022 film The Woman King with Viola Davis dramatized the Agojie. Ryan Coogler consulted Boston University Africanist scholars during pre-production. Florence Kasumba played Ayo and Danai Gurira played Okoye as the most-prominent Dora Milaje in Black Panther.

question: Thor: Ragnarok (2017) was Taika Waititi's first major-studio film. Waititi approached Marvel with a pitch focused on lightening the previously-serious Thor films. The film's iconic 'Immigrant Song' opening fight scene — Thor swinging Mjolnir as Led Zeppelin plays — required Marvel to pay one of the largest single-song licensing fees in studio history. The fee was negotiated personally with whom?
answer: Jimmy Page and Robert Plant, the surviving members of Led Zeppelin
choices: Jimmy Page and Robert Plant, the surviving members of Led Zeppelin
The estate of John Bonham via his son Jason Bonham, who acted as agent
Atlantic Records, the band's master-recording rights holder since 1968
Peter Grant Estate, since the band's original manager owned the rights
context: Led Zeppelin almost never grants song licenses. Page and Plant personally approved Ragnarok after watching an early cut Waititi sent them. The 'Immigrant Song' (1970, from Led Zeppelin III) plays both in the opening sequence and in the climactic Asgard-battle. Waititi's gambit was that the song's Norse mythology lyrical content ('We come from the land of the ice and snow') was uniquely thematic. The licensing fee has been variously reported at $1-2 million.

question: Avengers: Infinity War (2018) and Endgame (2019) were filmed back-to-back as one production from January 2017 to January 2018 — about 175 shooting days for two films. The Russos and writers Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely worked from a single megascript. The films' total budget was approximately $1 billion combined. The most-spoilered scene in Endgame's opening — the Avengers ambushing Thanos at his retirement farm — culminates in what specific Thor action that the Russos kept secret from most of the cast?
answer: Thor decapitating Thanos with Stormbreaker, going for the head this time
choices: Thor decapitating Thanos with Stormbreaker, going for the head this time
Thor binding Thanos in adamantine chains for Doctor Strange to extract Stones
Thor smashing Thanos's gauntlet to destroy the stones before they can be recovered
Thor calling lightning to teleport Thanos back to Vormir where Gamora could be returned
context: Thor's 'I went for the head' opening of Endgame is meta-commentary on his Infinity War failure (Stormbreaker stab to chest, didn't kill Thanos because Thanos completed the snap first). Hemsworth shot the scene with a stunt-double Brolin rather than the real Thanos. The Asgardian armor for the scene was a 60-pound suit. The film's opening was filmed last in the production schedule. The Russos kept the scene out of all marketing — opening night audiences experienced it cold.

question: Avengers: Endgame (2019)'s portal scene — where every dusted hero returns through Doctor Strange's sling-ring portals to join the final battle against Thanos's army — features the on-screen return of multiple characters in a single shot. Captain America's audio cue 'On your left' triggers the first portal opening. The scene took eleven months of pre-visualization and was originally planned to be Tony Stark's POV. Why was it shifted to Captain America's POV in final cut?
answer: The Russos felt 'On your left' was a more powerful callback to Cap's running-line from Winter Soldier
choices: The Russos felt 'On your left' was a more powerful callback to Cap's running-line from Winter Soldier
Downey Jr.'s schedule prevented him from completing his on-set close-ups for the original cut
Test audiences felt Cap's reaction shot was more emotional than Iron Man's during preview screenings
The original Iron Man cut was destroyed in a 2018 server corruption that lost three days of dailies
context: 'On your left' is Sam Wilson (Falcon)'s running-greeting line to Steve Rogers in the opening of Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014). Sam comes through the portal first, addressing Cap by radio. The shot composition — Cap kneeling and bloodied, then standing with Mjolnir and his shield — was inspired by classical heroic-painting compositions. The Russos screened the assembled scene for the entire cast at a wrap-party screening; multiple actors broke down in tears.

question: Marvel's Spider-Man Clone Saga ran across 100+ issues in five titles from 1994 to 1996, attempting to reset Peter Parker's continuity by revealing that the Spider-Man readers had been following since 1975 was actually a clone. The 'real' Peter was a character called Ben Reilly who had been wandering the country in exile for years under what name?
context: The Clone Saga was initially planned as a six-month story but expanded under executive pressure into a two-year crossover that sold millions but alienated longtime readers. Ben Reilly took over as Spider-Man for the better part of a year (1996) before Marvel reversed everything in 1997's Spider-Man #75. The Saga is widely considered the most-disliked Spider-Man storyline ever. Writer J.M. DeMatteis has spoken candidly about the editorial chaos that drove the storyline.

question: Phoenix Fawkes saves Harry's life multiple times in the Harry Potter series. In Chamber of Secrets, Fawkes brings Harry the Sorting Hat (which produces the Sword of Gryffindor) and then blinds the basilisk by pecking out its eyes. In Order of the Phoenix, Fawkes intervenes in Dumbledore's atrium duel with Voldemort by swallowing what specific magical attack to save Dumbledore?
choices: Voldemort's Crucio that would have shattered the Fountain statues
A controlled Fiendfyre conjured during the duel's middle phase
A Mind-Probing curse from Bellatrix that targeted Dumbledore's memory
context: Fawkes intercepts the green killing-curse beam at the Battle of the Department of Mysteries and dies, then is reborn from the ashes — a phoenix can absorb an Avada Kedavra. The atrium duel between Dumbledore and Voldemort is one of the most-cinematic moments in the entire series. The Order's name itself comes from Fawkes — Dumbledore's Patronus and personal-protector phoenix. The phoenix-feather wands of Harry and Voldemort both come from Fawkes's tail.
